title: Iranian men accused of spying targeted journalists for 'serious violence', court hears
description: Three Iranian men have gone on trial in London accused of spying for Iran on UK-based journalists, who were being targeted so "serious violence" could
body: Three Iranian men have gone on trial in London accused of spying for Iran on UK-based journalists, who were being targeted so "serious violence" could be inflicted on them.The prosecution said Mostafa Sepahvand, 41, was to carry out the attack, with Farhad Manesh, 46, and Shapoor Noori, 57, doing the surveillance and reconnaissance. All three were born in Iran but were living in London.The jury at Woolwich Crown Court heard that Sepahvand does not deny his involvement but said he did it out of fear of the consequences of refusing. The prosecution said that is "an entirely bogus claim", adding that he did it for money and to have a criminal conviction for theft in Iran "fixed".Sepahvand was in contact with two men with Iranian telephone numbers.According to the prosecution, Manesh and Noori are expected to say they did not know they were carrying out surveillance on behalf of Iran.All three face charges under the National Security Act, including "assisting a foreign intelligence service".Prosecutor Bill Emlyn Jones KC said the men's targets were journalists working for Iran International - a Persian-language satellite channel that is critical of the Tehran regime and has its headquarters in London.Jones said at least two journalists linked to Iran International were targeted in the surveillance.He said at least one of them was to be "subjected to serious violence" as retribution and "to try to silence and deter others who might dare to voice their criticism".Iran International, which broadcasts into Iran, has been declared as a "terrorist organisation" by Tehran."The evidence we will call illustrates that these three defendants carried out surveillance and reconnaissance, visiting addresses linked to their targets, taking photos, taking videos, doing online research about them," Jones said."The defendants were engaged in what is very obviously a form of spying," he added.The men also allegedly had a "briefing sheet" on a barrister, Jonathan Turner, who was a founding member of a group called UK Lawyers for Israel.One Iran International journalist who was allegedly targeted was Mojtaba Pourmohsen.Images of him, his workplace and a hotel where he had lived were found in a "briefing document" on Sepahvand's mobile phone.The prosecution says Noori took pictures of the block of flats Pourmohsen lived in in Brentford, southwest London, in December 2024. It is also alleged that Sepahvand and Manesh went there to take photos and videos.Jones said Sepahvand's motivation was to try to resolve a criminal conviction he had in Iran for theft."He was not just in it for money. He quite explicitly wants something very particular in return for his work - he wanted his criminal conviction in Iran to be fixed," Jones told the jury.The three men, who each had an interpreter in the dock, deny all the charges.All three were granted temporary leave to remain in the UK after claiming asylum. They arrived in the UK between 2016 and 2022. Sepahvand arrived in 2016 concealed in a lorry. The other two arrived in small boats.The trial continues.

schema.headline: Iranian men accused of spying targeted journalists for 'serious violence', court hears

title: Badenoch's £10bn air defence plan points to growing concern over protecting UK's skies
description: Currently the country has a number of systems to deal with short and medium-range threats – from drones to cruise missiles. But the armed forces still
body: Currently the country has a number of systems to deal with short and medium-range threats – from drones to cruise missiles. But the armed forces still lack a  weapons system to deal with long-range ballistic and hypersonic missiles. And those don't come cheap. Each interceptor used by the US Patriot missile system costs about $4m (£3m).Sophisticated air defences that can deal with a range of threats are expensive. The US Army alone wants to increase its budget for both missiles and interceptors  by fourfold next year – to $36bn (£27.1bn). Israel also spends a significant proportion of its $45bn (£33.9bn) annual military budget on  air defences.For the Conservatives there's also a presentation problem. Their original press release mentioned building a new air defence systems that would be "in essence, a British Iron Dome", referencing Israel's elaborate air defence system. But any comparison of the challenge of defending Britain's skies with Israel's, about 10% the size of the UK, is naive. Nor is the threat the same. Israel has regularly been targeted by drones and missiles over the past decade. The UK has not. The Conservatives now suggest the phrase "Iron Dome" was just a shorthand for better air defences. But even the words "Britannia Shield" may be a misnomer. It would be nigh on impossible for the UK to develop an air-defence system that could defend the whole country with such limited resources. At best it could afford a system to protect some key strategic sites – including military bases. At present the UK doesn't even have that.

schema.headline: Badenoch's £10bn air defence plan points to growing concern over protecting UK's skies

title: Former German spy chief arrested for espionage and treason
description: Former German spy chief August Hanning has been arrested on suspicion of espionage, treason and obtaining classified information for a foreign power,
body: Former German spy chief August Hanning has been arrested on suspicion of espionage, treason and obtaining classified information for a foreign power, the German Federal Prosecutor's Office says.Hanning headed the Federal Intelligence Service (BND) from 1998 to 2005 and has since been working as a private consultant. Prosecutors allege that he used classified intelligence to "draft an analysis" for one foreign intelligence service and maintained contact with another foreign spying service. Investigators have not disclosed which foreign powers were involved. Police also arrested former BND employee Manfred D, accusing him of passing Hanning about 2,000 classified documents for money.Manfred D, who was Hanning's bureau chief and remained in the BND until this year, is charged with aiding and abetting attempted treason and treasonous espionage.Local media reported Hanning was arrested at his home in Nordwalde near Münster while Manfred D was arrested in Bavaria. Hanning is due in court on Wednesday and Manfred D will appear on Tuesday.Prosecutors say Manfred D, who also served as the chief of staff for Hanning's successors between 2012 and 2026, used his role to gain access to highly confidential information which he then passed on to Hanning "in exchange for remuneration". "The current findings suggest that, over the years, Manfred D provided Hanning with approximately 2,000 documents, many of which contained classified information to be used exclusively by the Federal Intelligence Service for internal purposes," the statement says. "On one occasion, Hanning used classified intelligence ... to draft an analysis for an officer of a foreign intelligence service," prosecutors said, noting it was not clear if "the material reached the intended recipient".Hanning is also accused of being "in close contact with a representative of another foreign intelligence service, to whom he passed on political information, partially based on material provided by Manfred D, for several years". Local media say Hanning's alleged possession of intelligence documents came to light during a separate case relating to German steakhouse heiress Christina Block.Hamburg public prosecutor's office accused Block of orchestrating the kidnapping of her two youngest children in 2023 due to a custody dispute. Investigators allege Hanning was involved in an earlier attempted kidnapping of the children, which he denies.State criminal police officers reportedly discovered an electronic data storage device containing sensitive information including recent BND documents.It is not the first time the BND has faced similar controversy. A high-ranking German intelligence officer was charged with treason in 2023 for allegedly passing state secrets to Russia.Prosecutors alleged Carsten L shared intelligence about the war in Ukraine and the Wagner mercenary group and received roughly €400,000 ($450,000; £340,000). His trial is ongoing.

schema.headline: Former German spy chief arrested for espionage and treason

title: 'Ghost particles' from space telescope wins 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics
description: Belgian-born physicist Prof Francis Halzen has won the Nobel Prize in Physics for his pioneering work on an observatory that detects particles from sp
body: Belgian-born physicist Prof Francis Halzen has won the Nobel Prize in Physics for his pioneering work on an observatory that detects particles from space, shedding light on the distant universe.Halzen led the development of IceCube at the South Pole, which uses a cubic kilometre of Antarctic ice fitted with light sensors to detect particles called neutrinos. These carry information about violent, high-energy processes in the cosmos.The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences said "his vision and scientific leadership have been fundamental for the IceCube Neutrino Observatory".He first presented his vision for detecting neutrinos at the South Pole in 1988.Halzen, who is now a US citizen at the University of Wisconsin–Madison, told a news conference that he was surprised his idea worked so well."I have to emphasise how lucky I was. Because when we started this project, everybody realised this was maybe a good idea, but very few thought it would work, including myself."Neutrinos are elusive subatomic particles. The Sun produces vast numbers of them: every second, billions pass harmlessly through an area the size of your fingernail.But IceCube is searching for much higher-energy neutrinos, those produced by violent processes far beyond our Solar System — in distant galaxies. It is composed of thousands of sensors on long cables that are drilled and frozen into a 1km cubic block of ice.Neutrinos can be thought of as astronomical messengers that point to those fundamental events.At the observatory, most neutrinos pass straight through the ice, but occasionally one interacts with it, producing particles that give off a telltale flash of light.These rare signals carry clues to where the neutrinos came from and the extreme conditions that produced them — allowing scientists to investigate places that ordinary telescopes cannot easily see."Francis Halzen has led an international team of researchers and engineers who have provided us with a fantastic instrument," said Prof Mark Pearce, Chair of the Nobel Committee for Physics."His tenacity and scientific vision has paved the way for a new kind of astronomy." On the rare occasions when a neutrino strikes an atomic nucleus, it produces fast-moving charged particles. It is these racing through the ice, which give off a blue glow, which sensitive light detectors can pick up.The pattern and timing of that light allow scientists to estimate the direction the neutrino came from — helping them trace its origins in the cosmos. But these interactions are so rare that the observatory needed an enormous volume of clear ice.Halzen's idea was to use a vast natural ice sheet in Antarctica. So began an audacious plan to build a neutrino observatory at the geographic South Pole, with thousands of light sensors embedded deep in the ice.The neutrino's ghostly nature, the very thing that makes it so hard to detect, also makes it a powerful messenger from the distant Universe. Neutrinos rarely interact with material in its way, so they can go right through dense regions that light cannot easily penetrate. And because they have no electric charge, magnetic fields do not bend their paths through space. That means their direction of arrival can point scientists back towards their source.Their energies carry further insight into the processes that created them - helping scientists investigate how exploding stars and the environments around giant black holes accelerate particles to extraordinary energies. Louis Barson, director of science at the Institute of Physics in London, said the IceCube Observatory had enabled astronomers to investigate phenomena that conventional telescopes cannot see."The discoveries that have followed are helping us understand some of the most energetic and mysterious processes in the universe - and that's thanks to Professor Halzen's work," he added.Prof Subir Sarkar, physicist from the University of Oxford, quoted the French novelist Marcel Proust in describing his assessment of Halzen's contribution to science:"'The only true voyage of discovery, the only fountain of Eternal Youth, would be not to visit strange lands but to possess other eyes, to behold the universe through the eyes of another, of a hundred others, to behold the hundred universes that each of them beholds, that each of them is'."Francis Halzen has led the IceCube collaboration on just such a voyage of discovery and opened a new window on to our Universe".

schema.headline: 'Ghost particles' from space telescope wins 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics

title: UK to make last-ditch effort to stop Israel closing East Jerusalem consulate
description: The UK government is making a last-ditch attempt to persuade Israel not to close the British consulate in East Jerusalem later this week.Israel said i
body: The UK government is making a last-ditch attempt to persuade Israel not to close the British consulate in East Jerusalem later this week.Israel said in September that it would shut the mission, which is separate from the UK embassy based in Tel Aviv, in retaliation for the UK announcing sanctions on illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.British sanctions will ban settlement goods but also act against companies and individuals providing services for settlement expansion.The Foreign Office said it would not comment on "speculation and live discussions" that the UK could expel Israeli diplomats in response.The Israeli government said it would close the mission within 30 days of the UK sanctions announcement, meaning that the mission - first established in 1838 - will close on Thursday unless a deal is reached.The consulate handles UK relations with Palestinians in the city as well as in the West Bank and Gaza.UK National Security Adviser Jonathan Powell made an undisclosed visit to Israel last week for talks but seemingly left without reaching an agreement.According to Israeli media, the UK is threatening to expel up to 27 Israeli diplomats if the closure goes ahead.Such a tit-for-tat expulsion of diplomats is more common among adversaries than allies.France and Canada joined the UK in the initial sanctions, but Israel has not taken action against them.Emily Thornberry, chair of the foreign affairs committee, said: "Beyond the fact that the closure of the British consulate in East Jerusalem - occupied Palestinian territory - is not in Israel's prerogative, it is yet another attempt by this far-right Israeli government to block a two-state solution."She added: "It is illegal, and the UK must resist it."Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has previously said that they do not want the consulate to close."It would damage the very important work that we are doing, helping people in those communities," he said last month.

schema.headline: UK to make last-ditch effort to stop Israel closing East Jerusalem consulate

title: Defence lawyer in Cornell University case calls for special prosecutor Letitia James to be removed
description: A lawyer for one of the seven men accused of participating in a Cornell University gang rape has called for the special prosecutor on the case to recu
body: A lawyer for one of the seven men accused of participating in a Cornell University gang rape has called for the special prosecutor on the case to recuse herself over past public comments.The lawyer had said a social media post from New York Attorney General Letitia James throws into question her investigation's "integrity and independence".In the 28 September post, James wrote that "what this young woman has been forced to endure is horrific and unacceptable" and told survivors that "we stand with you".The university's administration is under fire over its alleged mishandling of the October 2024 incident and, according to US media, now faces a no-confidence vote by Cornell faculty. The university's Faculty Senate, a governing body comprised of professors and other academic staff, will vote on a resolution of no confidence next week, according to reports. A majority no-confidence vote would be a largely symbolic gesture, signalling the broader faculty's discontent and applying pressure on university leadership to act.The BBC has reached out to Cornell University for comment.Allegations made in a lawsuit against seven men and the Ivy League university have rocked the campus in New York state, with hundreds of students and faculty members gathering there on Monday in protest, and sparked anger across the country.New York Governor Kathy Hochul last week appointed James as a special prosecutor to investigate the case and how law enforcement and the university initially responded to the allegations made by a woman identified in the lawsuit as Jane Doe.Jane Doe has accused the university of failing to protect her, after she was allegedly drugged and raped by the men for several hours at a fraternity party. Days before she was appointed special prosecutor, James wrote on X: "What this young woman has been forced to endure is horrific and unacceptable. "I'm holding her in my heart and in my prayers," she continued. "To her, and to all survivors: you're not alone. We stand with you."The lawyer for one of the seven accused said these remarks were disqualifying. In a statement sent to the BBC's US media partner, CBS News, the lawyer said her comments conflict with the need for "independently evaluating the evidence"."This is not an accusation that Attorney General James is corrupt, acting in bad faith or incapable of performing her duties professionally," the statement said. "Nor am I suggesting that a court has determined that she is legally disqualified. The point is much narrower: an avoidable question now hangs over this investigation, and voluntary recusal would remove it."Governor Hochul and James were questioned about impartiality concerns during a news conference, and Hochul said James would "follow the facts". "She'll examine the evidence and go wherever it leads, and if the evidence supports charges, she will pursue them," Hochul said.

schema.headline: Defence lawyer in Cornell University case calls for special prosecutor Letitia James to be removed

title: Childminder who left 27 children alone in her home pleads guilty to neglect
description: Figure caption, Amanda Mathewson leaves Kirkcaldy Sheriff CourtByBen PhilipBBC ScotlandReporting fromKirkcaldy Sheriff Court and Megan BonarBBC Scotla
body: Figure caption, Amanda Mathewson leaves Kirkcaldy Sheriff CourtByBen PhilipBBC ScotlandReporting fromKirkcaldy Sheriff Court and Megan BonarBBC ScotlandUpdated 3 hours agoA Dunfermline childminder has admitted leaving more than 20 children she was caring for alone and unsupervised in her home.Amanda Mathewson, 55, pleaded guilty at Kirkcaldy Sheriff Court to neglect and abandoning children in her care.Her offending took place at a number of locations in Dunfermline and elsewhere in Fife.The court heard Mathewson had 27 children in her home, 19 more than she was licensed to look after.Mathewson, who has been a self-employed childminder for 30 years, was arrested by police following allegations of cruelty towards children.The court heard she had provided childcare services at her home in Dunfermline for children under the age of 16.At the time of her arrest she had 15 children aged under 12, 10 children under primary school age, and two children under the age of one in her care.Procurator fiscal Vicki Bell told the court two parents became suspicious of Mathewson after being informed their children were not present while the childminder carried out a school run.They secretly went to the school and found their children were not with Mathewson, despite being in her care.They then went to her home, where they heard a "child screaming" and found five unattended children in the garden.One of the children told the witnesses there were no adults inside, and Mathewson had told them to "wait in the garden".They approached the door of the house to check if there were any adults present, when they hear another child "screaming hysterically" inside.The door was unlocked, and when the witnesses entered they found a child crying under the kitchen table.A further nine children, all under five, were found in an upstairs bedroom. Two of them were strapped into prams. The children were said to be "distressed" but uninjured.Police attended and Mathewson said the children had been left alone for at least 30 minutes.The court heard ring doorbell footage showed it was the second time that day the children had been left inside the house.Dirty nappies and hungry, thirsty childrenDuring the police investigation, various children told their parents that being left alone in Mathewson's home was "commonplace".Some parents told officers that their children became "upset" when they were taken to the childminder's home and those who could talk would say they did not want to go.The investigation found discrepancies in the number of children in Matthewson's care and the number of children she was seen with on multiple occasions.For example, Mathewson attended a church Christmas party with three children, despite having nine kids in her care that day.The parents of the three children who were in attendance were sent a photo of their child with Santa, while the others were just sent a generic photo.There were other occasions such as a sports day and a visit to Dunfermline fire station where Mathewson was seen with fewer children than she was responsible for.Parents also raised concerns that their children had not eaten while in the childminder's care due to their clothes staying in "pristine condition" and it was a general theme that their children would return home thirsty.Some parents also reported their children returned home in dirty nappies or with dry faeces in their underwear.Court documents state that Mathewson always had loud music playing and did not let parents enter her home at drop off time in an attempt to "conceal how oversubscribed she was".When the childminder was asked about the number of children in her care, or the whereabouts of certain children she claimed she was being assisted by a "child-minding friend".Image source, GoogleImage caption, The case was heard at at Kirkcaldy Sheriff CourtMathewson admitted wilfully neglecting, abandoning and exposing children to a manner likely to cause them unnecessary suffering or injury to their health.The court heard she offered childcare places for more children than she could reasonably provide care for at the time.A Care Inspectorate report published in August 2023 said Mathewson was registered to provide care for a maximum of eight children at any one time.It included conditions that a maximum of six children could be under the age of 12, no more than three could have started primary school, and no more than one could be under 12-months-old.The unannounced inspection from about a year before her arrest had rated areas including care, learning and the setting as "very good", the second-highest level in the quality scale.The report said "children were cared for in a comfortable, welcoming and homely environment" and "were cared for with warmth, kindness and a nurturing approach".A spokesperson for the Care Inspectorate said this is a "distressing case" and they have "implemented changes as a result of learning from this case."In a statement given to the BBC, one of the parents said: "The criminal case is important for justice.  But our ultimate goal is to ensure no other family has to endure what we have been through.  Our trust was broken, but our resolve is not."We have turned our pain into a purpose: to rebuild the system of childcare regulation and family support so that it is truly fit to protect Scotland's children."Sheriff John MacRitchie deferred sentencing until 6 November to allow background reports to be carried out. Mathewson's bail was continued.

schema.headline: Childminder who left 27 children alone in her home pleads guilty to neglect

title: Jeffrey Archer: Queen Camilla pays tribute to 'irrepressible' author and former politician
description: Archer sold more than 300 million books in his five-decade writing career, including the Clifton Chronicles and Kane and Abel, and often set the novel
body: Archer sold more than 300 million books in his five-decade writing career, including the Clifton Chronicles and Kane and Abel, and often set the novels in his home town of Wellington, Somerset.In a statement, Archer's publisher HarperCollins said the author died "suddenly and peacefully at home" on Monday between writing sessions.Archer was born in north London in 1940 but soon moved to Weston-super-Mare in Somerset and in 1969, Archer was elected MP for the Lincolnshire constituency of Louth.He served as an MP for five years before becoming Conservative Party deputy chairman.He moved to the House of Lords in 1992 but was jailed for four years for perjury and perverting the course of justice in 2001.He was found to have lied in libel action he had brought against the Daily Star newspaper, in which he was awarded £500,000 in damages.The Star had alleged Archer had slept with a sex worker.The peer was found by the court to have perverted the course of justice by asking a former friend to give him a false alibi and producing fake diary entries to back up his story.He was also found to have perjured himself on oath during the libel trial.He was released from jail in 2003 and returned to the House of Lords until he retired in 2024.Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch described Archer's death as "devastating news"."We will miss him very much," she told BBC Breakfast on Tuesday, adding that he had texted her earlier on Monday.Badenoch said he was "very much loved by the Conservative family", adding: "I'm glad that I saw him recently."Speaking about what she described as "other parts of his life", she said: "He did serve his time, he made amends, and he wanted to do a lot of good in the world."Former Conservative prime minister Sir John Major said "we have lost a man who lived one of the most remarkable lives of our age", and that he will be "much missed – and long remembered".Archer's last novel, Adam and Eve, was released on Tuesday.Broadcaster Gyles Brandreth told BBC Breakfast that he was with Archer on Sunday. "I mean, literally 72 hours ago, doing a show in the West End of London celebrating this book, the publication, and he was in great form."He didn't really acknowledge that he'd changed much since being in prison, but I think he became a nicer person in some ways, a gentler, a milder person after the prison experience."Former Conservative Party leader Iain Duncan Smith described Archer as "a remarkable man who did everything at full bore", adding: "There were simply no half measures with him."Other former ministers also paid tribute. Sajid Javid said Archer had been a "dear friend", while Sir Jeremy Hunt said Archer had "showed enormous kindness with his advice about how to become a writer".James Cleverly said the author and politician had been "a huge personality and fantastic storyteller", and that he had been very supportive when his wife Suzie was recovering from cancer.Reform UK member and former Conservative minister Nadim Zahawi, wrote: "Jeffrey Archer was a dear friend and an extraordinary human being. His gift for storytelling was matched by his wit, warmth and boundless energy. Life was never dull in Jeffrey's company."

schema.headline: Jeffrey Archer: Queen Camilla pays tribute to 'irrepressible' author and former politician

title: Victor Wembanyama: NBA star trains with rugby club
description: NBA superstar Victor Wembanyama says he was inspired by the unity and camaraderie of rugby after spending part of his summer off-season training with
body: NBA superstar Victor Wembanyama says he was inspired by the unity and camaraderie of rugby after spending part of his summer off-season training with French second tier side Provence.The 22-year-old Frenchman, who is 7ft 4in and 16st 11lbs, is known for his off-beat search for ways to improve his game. He spent a fortnight focusing on physical and mental strength with Shaolin monks in China in 2025., externalFootage shows Wembanyama, external hitting tackle pads, going through passing drills, taking part in a line-out and looming over the rest of the Provence team in a huddle before a pre-season friendly in August.He was also filmed sharing a dressing-room embrace with former England international Teimana Harrison, who won five England caps in 2016 and now plays for Provence."It was a great experience, seeing the team spirit they have over there," said Wembanyama,, external who was joined on the trip by San Antonio Spurs' team-mate Harrison Barnes."It was very inspiring to see the relationship between team-mates, coaches and fans. The training was really hard, really good for stability, movement patterns and developing strength, but I am more grateful for the experience of how I was welcomed there. "I have never been welcomed anywhere like this. I wasn't part of the team but they treated me like I was. I want to do it again."Wembanyama combined his work with Provence with hosting his Hoop Gambit event, in which participants play games of chess and basketball, in his hometown of Le Chesnay.Wembanyama's Spurs fell just short of the NBA Championship earlier this year, going down 4-1 to the New York Knicks in June.Provence, who previously have been represented by Wales internationals George North and Tomas Francis, have begun their season and search for promotion to the Top 14 well, winning their first five league games.

schema.headline: Victor Wembanyama: NBA star trains with rugby club

title: Paramount takes over Warner Bros in $110bn Hollywood merger
description: Paramount Skydance has officially taken over Warner Bros Discovery in a $110bn merger that is set to reshape Hollywood and the media landscape. The ta
body: Paramount Skydance has officially taken over Warner Bros Discovery in a $110bn merger that is set to reshape Hollywood and the media landscape. The takeover - merging two of the biggest studios in Los Angeles - comes after months of legal disputes and widespread criticism over feared cuts and consolidation could harm competition and consumers. It will alter streaming for millions, usher in a new chapter in the film and TV industry, and leave one of the biggest US news outlets, CNN, in uncertain territory.The merger will also bring together a host of entities including HBO, CBS, Nickelodeon, Showtime, Comedy Central, DC Studios and Food Network. Paramount will acquire ownership of iconic franchises that include Harry Potter, Game of Thrones, The Lord of the Rings and Mission: Impossible. The newly merged entertainment behemoth will be re-branded under the name Skydance Corporation, the company originally founded by David Ellison before he took over both Paramount and Warner Bros Discover. Ellison, chairman and chief executive of Skydance, said the completion of the deal was "historic" for the film industry."From the start, our ambition was to bring these two storied studios together and create a stronger competitor, with the talent, resources, and reach to tell great stories in every genre, on every platform, for audiences everywhere. Now that ambition is a reality," he said.Last week, Ellison named the outgoing chief executive of Mattel, Ynon Kreiz, as co-chief executive.Kreiz will focus on the company's day-to-day operations, including integrating the  newly-combined businesses, while Ellison will focus on strategy and technology.Mark Thompson - who once served as director general of the BBC - will continue in his role as chairman and editor-in-chief of CNN Worldwide, while Bari Weiss remains editor-in-chief of CBS News.Casey Bloys, who has lead HBO and Max Content, will be the co-chair and chief content officer for direct-to-consumer content. Mike Proulx, research director at Forrester Research, said that change "essentially means the HBO leadership team is now in charge of Skydance's combined streaming operation". "While that bodes well for the HBO brand, make no mistake, Bloys will be pressured to find and deliver cost efficiencies that could affect content quality," he warned.While the company said it had received unanimous approval from competition authorities across the world, the long running takeover process has featured controversy since the beginning.Netflix initially had a deal to buy part of Warner Bros Discovery, but Paramount Skydance launched a bidding war, leading to the streaming giant walking away. Lawyers in about a dozen US states then filed lawsuits - led by California - aiming to block the deal, arguing it would stifle competition, raise consumer prices and cause "substantial" harm to movie theatres, cable distributors and "ultimately, audiences nationwide". US states announced a settlement with Paramount and Ellison last month which paved the way for the merger to go ahead.As part of the deal, Paramount has agreed to establish a "news editorial independence board" to "ensure independent, objective, fact-based reporting" at CNN and CBS.Politics and editorial independence has become an area of concern at CBS since the news broadcaster was taken over in 2025 as part of separate a merger between Skydance Media and Paramount.Ellison, who hosted a dinner for President Donald Trump earlier this year, has sought to reassure people that editorial independence will be maintained.Over its 103-year-old history, Warner Bros has won more than 100 Academy Awards - including dominating at last year's show with a record-tying 11 Oscars for One Battle After Another, Sinners and Weapons.Paramount traces its roots back 1912 and also boasts more than 100 Oscars for classics spanning from The Godfather to Titanic, though the studio has not mirrored the same recent spate of Hollywood honours. The studio was not nominated for any projects last year by the Academy. Its last win came in 2022 with Top Gun: Maverick. The deal with US states aims to ensure the merged studios will produce "real, robust movies" that will generate economic activity and put people back to work, said California Attorney General Rob Bonta, who led the lawsuit and settlement. To prevent the studio from fulfilling its annual quota with low-budget or automated content, the deal includes strict guardrails against "AI-generated" films.As part of the agreement, Paramount must release at least 30 films each year. If it fails to meet its annual production quota, it will be forced to sell its 49% stake in Miramax, the film company founded by disgraced Hollywood mogul Harvey Weinstein and his brother Bob.Paramount also must ensure 20% of all film production takes place in the US for the first two years, rising to more than 30% through the following three years.

schema.headline: Paramount takes over Warner Bros in $110bn Hollywood merger

title: Dread presenting at work? Read these tips before your next meeting
description: Image source, Studio Grey for Social Market FoundationImage caption, Dani Payne would have panic attacks at the thought of presenting - now she does i
body: Image source, Studio Grey for Social Market FoundationImage caption, Dani Payne would have panic attacks at the thought of presenting - now she does it most daysByEmily HoltUpdated 3 hours agoDani Payne was so anxious about public speaking, she had a doctor's note to excuse her from presenting at school and university.Now aged 28 with a job in politics at a cross-party think tank, she's spoken in parliament, sits on discussion panels and presents social media videos. "Most days I do some form of public speaking," she says. "I wouldn't have believed that at 15."Want to get better, or simply get started? Here are four ways to help you nail your presentation or speech.Woman's HourSpeaking in Public: Why it feels so hard to do and how to do it anyway. Listen now.1. Start with your passionPayne, from Exeter, says she stopped any form of public speaking after developing a severe anxiety disorder and experiencing panic attacks.But looking back, she says avoiding it didn't help her build "coping skills or resilience". "The more you avoid what you're anxious about, the more you're anxious about it."In her second year of university she was invited to present a subject she was passionate about. "I realised I was losing out on opportunities that I felt really strongly about."She presented research for her dissertation on sexual misconduct in academic fieldwork settings and that was the start of conquering her fear.Her advice is to look for or create opportunities to speak about something you care about. "Picking something you genuinely feel passionately about will always make it easier," she says. 2. Practise in virtual realityImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, A virtual reality headset can help you present in front of a pretend audienceDaisy Schofield, a 32-year-old documentary producer and journalist, had her first panic attack at university during a presentation, she tells Woman's Hour.She managed to avoid public speaking until she got her first job and had to present company statistics on Teams every Monday. To build her confidence, Schofield practises by using an app on her phone to create a fake audience in a virtual reality headset she bought online for £10. "It makes practising feel much more engaging and like the real thing, compared to practising at home on your own, which feels a bit awkward and boring."3. Choose one wordImage source, Fred Ferschke for EmotionImage caption, Stand-up comedian Viv GroskopViv Groskop,  a stand-up comedian, writer and public speaking coach advises picking a word that encapsulates what you want your speech to convey. "It could be something like clarity... you can think to yourself afterwards, 'did I set out to be clear? Was I clear? Yes. It's a win.' And every time you choose a different word."Groskop also advises putting a post-it note on your laptop camera and reminding yourself to look there and not at people on the screen "because it will mean you're looking down, not at people."When you're presenting in person, Prof Nazanin Derakhshan, a neuroscientist at Birkbeck, University of London, advises not to focus too much on people's faces."Accept that their facial expression may mean anything, and distract yourself internally from interpreting these facial expressions."4. Expect mistakesPayne says being good at public speaking does not come "naturally to someone"."You wouldn't pick up a guitar, and be surprised that you couldn't play a song when you've never picked up a guitar before - public speaking is the exact same thing."Groksop says people who are good at public speaking have just been doing it more."Many people are spending up to eight hours a day on Teams or Zoom, and if you think about a television newsreader, they've been trained for that."She says no one around you expects you to "immediately be a master public speaker the first time you do it".Derakhshan says being vulnerable is a "big asset" when public speaking. "We all make mistakes, we all forget things. It's not the end of the world. If you can go back and make a humour of it the audience are quite forgiving and accepting."Additional Reporting by Simon Richardson.

schema.headline: Dread presenting at work? Read these tips before your next meeting

title: LIV Golf: Competition secures potential $300m investment to emerge from restructuring
description: LIV Golf has secured a possible $300m in financing from BC Partners Credit in order to try to move forward with the 2027 season.The league filed for C
body: LIV Golf has secured a possible $300m in financing from BC Partners Credit in order to try to move forward with the 2027 season.The league filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in the United States in September after Saudi Arabia withdrew its multibillion-dollar funding, starting a court-supervised "restructuring process" that they hope to complete in early 2027.It is unclear how much of the $300m LIV requires to start next year's schedule and which players will start the season.The competition's participants are owed at least $45m (£33m) and have the option to leave.However the agreement secures an extension for the league to discuss terms with its players, with talks now open until 25 October.BBC Sport understands there is no obligation on players to sign on to LIV 2.0, regardless of whether they had previously signed multi-year contracts with LIV Golf.League insiders see the committed investment as a "significant" step forward in the court-supervised restructuring process."Our goal is to facilitate LIV Golf's emergence from the restructuring process on sound financial footing and with renewed momentum heading into the 2027 season," said Ted Goldthorpe, partner and head of BC Partners Credit, in a statement.The credit firm, which provides financing to middle-market companies, said the funding would support the next phase of LIV Golf, under which players would become equity owners of both the league and its teams.The financing remains subject to bankruptcy court approval and customary conditions."This investment is an important step forward for LIV Golf," said LIV Golf CEO Scott O'Neil in a statement."We're delivering on our major milestones, and while there is still work ahead, today marks meaningful progress toward a player-owned, team-focused, truly global league that complements the wider game and creates new opportunities for players, fans, partners, and the next generation of golfers."Since LIV's controversial launch in 2021, more than $5bn (£3.7bn) has been spent by Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund (PIF), with major winners including Jon Rahm and Bryson DeChambeau lured by lucrative contracts and vast prize money.However, the future of the concept - and its star players - has been shrouded in uncertainty, with the 2026 season having ended early.Documents in the petition outline money owed to LIV Golf's creditors with the 30 largest unsecured claims. Two-time major winner Rahm tops that list with an unsecured claim of $7.5m (£5.5m).DeChambeau ($5.7m - £4.2m), Dustin Johnson ($5.5m - £4.1m), Cameron Smith ($4.8m - £3.5m) and Tyrrell Hatton ($3.4m - £2.5m) are also among the top 30 creditors, as well as Brooks Koepka, who left to rejoin the PGA Tour in January but has an unsecured claim of $1.7m (£1.25m).The total amount owed to the 14 current and former LIV players in the top 30 creditors is just over $45m (£33m).A source familiar with the figures told BBC Sport the creditors list outlines the "amount owed and not paid for Q3" of 2026, not the full amounts.Chapter 11 protection postpones a US company's obligations to its creditors, giving it time to reorganise its debts or sell parts of the business.PIF is providing a bankruptcy loan of $49.6m (£36.6m) - called 'debtor in possession' (DIP) financing - to help fund the process.

schema.headline: LIV Golf: Competition secures potential $300m investment to emerge from restructuring

title: NFL: Officials Jeff Seeman and Adrian Hill suspended for player incidents
description: The NFL has suspended two officials for instances of unprofessional conduct towards a player.Line judge Jeff Seeman has been suspended for two games a
body: The NFL has suspended two officials for instances of unprofessional conduct towards a player.Line judge Jeff Seeman has been suspended for two games and referee Adrian Hill for one fixture following the incidents on Sunday.Seeman was caught on camera seeming to curse at Arizona Cardinals tight end Trey McBride, whose side lost 36-24 away to the New York Giants.McBride felt he had been interfered with by Giants cornerback Dru Phillips from a pass from Cardinals quarterback Jacoby Brissett that fell incomplete. Having been hit, McBride complained to Seeman, who appeared to yell a profanity at McBride."It's a tough one for me. You hate to see it for obvious reasons. I don't need to go further than that, but I do want to give the man a little bit of grace too," Cardinals coach Mike LaFleur said Monday. "I know Jeff. He's a good man. It's unfortunate it happened. It can't happen obviously and I'll leave it at that."Hill's incident involved linebacker Eric Wilson, who featured for Minnesota Vikings as they defeated the visiting Miami Dolphins 15-10.Wilson was pushed into Hill by Dolphins running back Ollie Gordon II midway through the first quarter after a play was whistled dead because of a Minnesota penalty.

schema.headline: NFL: Officials Jeff Seeman and Adrian Hill suspended for player incidents

title: China Open: Novak Djokovic claims 102nd career title, Carlos Alcaraz wins Japan trophy
description: Earlier, Alcaraz won the Japan Open, claiming a trophy in just his third tournament since injuring his wrist in April.The Spaniard came back from an e
body: Earlier, Alcaraz won the Japan Open, claiming a trophy in just his third tournament since injuring his wrist in April.The Spaniard came back from an early break down to beat Czech Jiri Lehecka 7-6 (7-4) 6-4 and successfully defend his title in Tokyo.Alcaraz only returned to competitive tennis at August's US Open, where he reached the quarter-finals before losing in five tight sets to Ben Shelton.It is Alcaraz's third title of the season, having won the Australian Open in January to complete the career Grand Slam, and also February's Qatar Open."It's extra special after my injury," the 25-year-old said."It was a tough week that I didn't find my best tennis, my best level, but I did find the good solutions. "I think that's what matters in the end."

title: Lionel Messi: Argentina legend has big plans for the future as golden era ends
description: Lionel Messi is about to play his last match for Argentina.On what will be his 208th appearance, the country's most-capped player and record goalscore
body: Lionel Messi is about to play his last match for Argentina.On what will be his 208th appearance, the country's most-capped player and record goalscorer will bid an emotional farewell in a friendly against Benin at the Monumental in Buenos Aires on Tuesday (Wednesday 00:00 BST).Arguably Argentina's greatest ever player - only Diego Maradona comes close -  announced his retirement from the national team on 31 August, six weeks after the World Cup final defeat by Spain, saying he had nothing more to give. Coach Lionel Scaloni insists that if Messi ever wants to carry on, he can, and there is no embarrassment in changing one's mind. But that chapter seems closed.His club career though goes on. The contract with Inter Miami runs to the end of the 2028 season, but it is reviewed year by year, and nobody close to him expects him to walk away a day before he has to. In fact, it is quite likely he will renew it if he feels, mentally and physically, up for it.Ask the people around him what comes after that and they smile, because Messi has never really planned beyond his next game. Even so, the shape of what lies ahead is already in front of us. He will stay inside football, because he would struggle to live without it, but his other business interests stretch far outside the game.Messi used to like the idea of being a sporting director or an adviser to the president, close to the decisions without all the travelling and the phone calls. And asked recently whether he would rather be a coach or an owner, Messi chose owner. A coach lives and dies by every Saturday and has to worry about far too many things for Messi's liking.An owner shapes the direction of a club from a little further back. Having said that, he would be an owner who does not stop at approving the appointment of a manager and stepping away. He would want to be involved in everything.The groundwork is being laid in Spain. UE Cornella, on the edge of Barcelona and in the fifth tier, is the nursery where young players grow. He bought it in April. CD Eldense, in the second division, announced Messi as its new owner on 1 October, subject to authorisation from the Spanish sports council, the CSD. Eldense will be the club that leads his football operation, but the target this season is not to get relegated, so former Villarreal boss Javi Calleja got the job with the arrival of the new owner.The plan is to run both through people he trusts, who will act as a link between Messi and the clubs until the day he can give them his full attention. For now he follows every Eldense match closely on his computer. After Eldense beat Real Oviedo by four goals to one, his first message as owner was an Instagram post that read "Aupa Deportivo". The pull of his name has been felt as well. Around a dozen sponsors came forward within a couple of days, some of them brands that had been talking to the previous owners without ever closing a deal, and some that already have a relationship with him.In Uruguay he and Luis Suarez founded Deportivo LSM in May 2025, and they won promotion to the country's third tier in its first season. A network of more clubs was discussed at the start. But the sums needed to lift them up the divisions have cooled that idea quickly, and it is not on the table today. Messi's focus is to see whether Eldense can establish itself in La Liga.There is a link to Miami as well. As part of his contract with Inter Miami, he will have some shares in the club when he retires. A franchise of his own is not part of the plan.Could he go home to Newell's Old Boys, the club where he played as a child in Rosario? The idea has never been formally discussed. It may have crossed his mind while drinking mate with Suarez, in the way a return to Barcelona or a spell at Napoli, the club of Maradona, might have. Nobody close to the player expects it though. Everything is built around Europe and Miami, and the perfect home is waiting for the family in Castelldefels, close to the sea and Barcelona.Newell's will still be close, because the club is one of the sixteen academies at this year's Messi Cup.If owning clubs is one love, youth football is the other, and his regular presence at his son's games and the Messi Cup are the proof. He puts his money and his time into a tournament for Under-16 academies, which began in 2025 with eight teams.Last year, the organisers expected him to come to one or two games, perhaps only the final, but to everyone's surprise, he sat through every match on every day.This year the teams doubled to 16, from 25 October at Inter Miami's facilities in Florida, including Atletico Madrid, Chelsea, Barcelona, Inter Milan, Arsenal, UE Cornella, and others.Away from the pitch, Messi has built a portfolio that helps explain why Forbes put his net worth at about $1.1bn, external in June, with earnings of around $140m over the previous year split between football and business.His best known endorsement is the lifetime Adidas deal he signed in 2017. The most visible piece is MiM Hotels, six boutique properties from Ibiza to Andorra, which Melia has run under a rental agreement since 1 November 2025. MiM takes its name from Messi and the Majestic hotel group, and runs the hotels inside its Melia Collection.In Rosario, his family firm invests in Carrasco M, a development of 24 homes by the Parana river, with Ángel Di María's property agency handling the sales.He is also a partner in the restaurant chain El Club de la Milanesa which plans to open five branches in Catalonia, the first in Castelldefels. He has a mate collection with the drinkware giants Stanley, the brand's first multi-year deal with an athlete, and he gave his opinion on materials and colours.The business side began with his father. Jorge Messi, who died in August aged 68, looked after his son's affairs from the start, and some of his early advice led the family into trouble with the tax authorities in Spain. The company then grew into branches for TV production, marketing, media and commercial partnerships, among others, all well established by the time Jorge fell seriously ill.Messi trusts the people who run them, some of them with him since his early days at Barcelona, and a thorough filter means he only gets offered and chooses what he is comfortable with. He sets his own relationship with the business world, and nobody imposes anything on him.In Miami last November, Messi told the America Business Forum: "Business is something that interests me. I would like to keep learning because I know nothing and I am just starting out." The portfolio his circle has prepared is already impressive while he finds more football targets to keep the flame alive.

schema.headline: Lionel Messi: Argentina legend has big plans for the future as golden era ends
